strengths: The paper addresses an important application: user-level private federated training of large ASR models on naturally partitioned, heterogeneous speech data. The benchmark and training recipe could be useful to both speech and federated-learning researchers.

The empirical benefit of per-layer clipping is substantial. At the same noise level in Table 1, dimension-based clipping reduces English test WER from 31.1% to 20.4% compared with global clipping. This is a meaningful optimization insight even independently of the population extrapolation.

The experiments extensively examine initialization, domain shift, cohort size, data heterogeneity, optimizers, and augmentation. Transferring English hyperparameters to French and German provides useful evidence of robustness.

Public datasets, detailed training and accountant configurations, compute reporting, and a code link support reproducibility. The manuscript appropriately motivates user-level privacy and openly discloses its public-seed and extrapolation assumptions.
weaknesses: The central convergence corollary is not established. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1 − 8(1 − η_loc T_loc)^2 > 0, but its proposed η_loc = Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))) makes η_loc T_loc approach zero for fixed T_loc, so κ approaches −7. The bound therefore becomes vacuous in the claimed asymptotic regime. It also retains a nonvanishing DP-noise term, which does not establish the stated convergence to a stationary point.

The convergence proof contains additional substantive gaps. Equations (33)–(34) treat the LAMB scaling p_h^(t) as independent of the current Gaussian noise, although it is computed from the noisy update through the second moment and trust ratio. The factorization and cancellation of cross terms consequently need justification or replacement. Equation (20) also invokes bounded gradients from smoothness without establishing the required bounded-domain or bounded-iterate assumption.

The headline privacy–utility pairs are conditional projections rather than jointly demonstrated results. English measurements use 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024; the ε = 4.5 and 7.2 headline guarantees assume approximately 7 million and 70 million users, respectively, with cohorts of 204,800. The corresponding measured runs have ε around 10^7–10^8. The disclosure is welcome, but the non-private cohort-scaling experiments in Appendix H.10 do not validate preservation of utility under this joint scaling with DP noise. A controlled noisy scaling study would materially strengthen the practical claims.

The privacy accounting needs a precise match to the implemented mechanism. Algorithm 1 specifies independent Poisson sampling but says the implementation fixes cohort size, while the accountant assumes the former. Furthermore, Appendix I.1's equivalence between client-side and fixed-variance server-side Gaussian noise is not exact under random cohort sizes: conditional aggregate noise variance depends on the realized number of clients. These discrepancies require a matching accountant or an explicitly revised mechanism.

The claimed importance of combining LAMB with per-layer clipping is insufficiently isolated experimentally. Tables 8–9 compare optimizers without DP, and Appendix H.4 leaves Adam's numerical stabilizer untuned despite acknowledging its importance. A matched LAMB/Adam × global/per-layer clipping ablation under DP is needed to support the interaction claim. Repeated-run uncertainty is also missing, particularly for the small improvements reported in French and German.
